claims.claim: A pH electrode is a passive device whose current from hydrogen ion activity is too weak to be detected with a multimeter or an analog-to-digital converter, so only proper connectors and cables should be used.
claims.quote:
This current (which can be positive or negative) is very weak and cannot be
detected with a multimeter, or an analog to digital converter.

claims.claim: The current generated by hydrogen ion activity is the reciprocal of that activity and can be predicted by an equation whose terms are R the ideal gas constant, T the temperature in Kelvin, and F the Faraday constant.
claims.quote:
Where R is the ideal gas constant.
T is the temperature in Kelvin.
F is the Faraday constant.

claims.claim: Because a pH probe is passive it can pick up voltages transmitted through the solution being measured, which produces incorrect readings and slowly damages the probe over time, so proper isolation is required in that case.
claims.quote:
This will result in incorrect readings and will
slowly damage the pH probe over time. In this instance, proper isolation is required.

claims.claim: Repeated wetting and drying cycles will eventually damage the Industrial pH probe, so it should be kept wet at all times, though a probe left out to dry should not be considered damaged and only needs rehydrating.
claims.quote:
However, repeated wetting and drying cycles will eventually damage
the probe. For best results, keep the probe wet at all times.

claims.claim: If a pH probe is kept in a hot environment during shipping, KCl creep may form a salt channel that wicks water out of the probe's soaker bottle and dries it out.
claims.quote:
KCl will form a salt channel that wicks the water out of the probe's soaker

claims.claim: To rehydrate the Industrial pH probe: place it in a beaker of tap water, let it sit 3 to 5 minutes, add a scoop of KCl (best) or NaCl (good) to the beaker, then let it sit in the salt water 15 to 20 minutes.
claims.quote:
1. Place the probe into a beaker of tap water.
2. Let the probe sit in the water for 3 – 5 mins.
3. Add a scoop of KCL (best) or NaCl (good) to the beaker.

claims.claim: The salt-water soak step of the pH probe rehydration procedure lasts 15 to 20 minutes, after which the probe is ready to use.
claims.quote: 4. Let the probe sit in the salt water for 15 – 20 mins.

claims.claim: Coating of the pH bulb leads to erroneous readings including a shortened span (slope), and the type of coating determines the cleaning technique.

gaps: Gives no calibration procedure and names no calibration buffers: pH 4.00, 7.00 and 10.00 never appear, and there is no single-, two- or three-point sequence, no order of operations, and no rinse-between-buffers instruction.
Gives no slope or mV-per-pH figure, no isopotential point, and no acceptance criterion for a passing calibration — yet it repeatedly warns about 'shortened span (slope)' as a failure mode.
Gives no temperature compensation guidance and no coefficient, even though this is explicitly the No Temp variant with no internal temperature probe and a -5 to 99 C range.

The Nernst-type equation is referenced and its variables are defined (R, T, F) but the equation itself is an image and does not survive text extraction, so the corpus holds the variable list without the formula.
States accuracy as +/- 0.002 pH and resolution as +/- 0.001 pH with no dependence on temperature or position in the 0-14 range, and no distinction between the two figures' meaning.
Gives no drift rate and no criterion for deciding a reading has drifted enough to require recalibration or reconditioning.
Gives no composition for pH probe storage solution and no substitute if the bottle runs out; the rehydration procedure uses tap water plus KCl or NaCl, not storage solution.
Gives no pH values that indicate any water-quality condition — no healthy range for fresh or salt water, no environmental interpretation of any kind.
Gives no flow or stirring requirement for taking a reading and no settling or stabilization time before recording a value.
Names the 'Atlas Scientific pH probe reconditioning kit' but gives no reconditioning steps, no chemicals, and no part number.
Gives no maintenance interval distinct from the recalibration intervals; unlike the DO datasheet there is no consumable to replace and no '~18 months maintenance' figure.
summary.notes: Three-chunk document. Chunk 1 opens with ~400 characters of overlap repeating the Specifications block from chunk 0, and chunk 2 opens with overlap repeating the long-term-storage paragraph from chunk 1; claims are recorded only on the originating chunk. Two internal tensions: the spec table gives '~1 Year Time before recalibration' while the body says there is no set schedule, and the body both instructs 'keep the probe wet at all times' and allows up to 3 weeks dry. The front spec table's 'No Temp' label is a variant name, not a table row, so the no-internal-temperature-probe claim is anchored on the Specifications block instead. The operating-principle page ends in a long run of stray bullet and box glyphs, and 'defuse' (for diffuse) is a source spelling error preserved verbatim in the quote. Dimension figures on page 3 arrive as bare numbers with labels detached. This is the only probe datasheet in the set that states a tolerated dry-out period; the ORP datasheet says its probe must never be allowed to dry out.
